newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week--BoE inflation report holds key.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week--BoE inflation report holds key.

text.p: UK gilts should regain some confidence this week and may outperform skittish U.S. Treasuries as last week's UK rate rise eases market concern over the Bank of England's inflation report, analysts said.

Tension over U.S. elections and quarterly refunding there may also help close the gap, said Tom Rayner, gilts analyst at Societe Generale in London. By 1230 GMT on Monday, the 10-year spread over Treasuries was at 137 basis points.

Analysts expected the Bank of England to call for a further rise in interest rates in its November inflation report, due at 1130 GMT on Wednesday, and to reiterate that inflation is set to miss the government's 2.5 percent target over the medium-term.

But they added the pressure would be off Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to raise rates in the near term after the surprise 25 basis point increase in interest rates to 6.0 percent last week.

"The report may show some deterioration in short-term prospects, but looking further ahead, both higher base rates and the firmer currency are likely to result in a more sanguine tone," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.

With the March short sterling contract at 93.40, the market is already pricing in around a 50 basis point rise in rates by March next year. "The market is looking for further hikes now, so it will take something pretty special to get a reaction (from the report)," said Rayner.

Gilts and short sterling sold off last week after the rate rise and lost ground to Bunds. By 1230, GMT December gilt futures were trading on LIFFE at 108-24, down from 110-00 just prior to the rate rise.
The 10-year spread with Bunds stood at 182 basis points, 14 basis points wider than before the rate rise.

"There's a possibility of outperforming Bunds because 182 looks a bit too high," one analyst said. "It's a matter of the gilt market getting a little bit of confidence back after some disappointing numbers."
In terms of data, the market will scrutinise September industrial production figures and manufacturing output, both due at 0930 GMT on Tuesday.

According to a Reuter poll, analysts expect industrial production to rise 0.5 percent in September, giving a 0.2 percent year-on-year rise. Manufacturing output is seen rising 0.5 percent in September and 0.1 percent on the same period a year ago.

"Survey information suggests that industrial production bounced back in September, largely due to strong domestic orders rather than a pick-up in export demand," said Schroders economist David Philpotts.
"In fact, the recovery from recession has almost entirely been a domestic story, suggesting growth is assured regardless of sterling's recent behaviour."
Rayner said the manufacturing data would do nothing to halt the recent flattening trend in UK gilts.

Analysts said the Confederation of British Industry distributive trades survey, due in the early hours of Thursday morning, would confirm the picture of strengthening consumer spending in the UK economy. They added it was unlikely to be market supportive.
Adding to gilt market uncertainty this week was potential fall-out from the U.S. elections on Tuesday, analysts said.
Though victory for incumbent President Clinton seems assured, the market remains concerned that the Democrats will gain the balance of power in both the House and the Senate.
"We can't detach ourselves completely from the U.S....there may be a knock-on effect but it won't be the key for us." said Societe General's Rayner.
